The sickly-sweet utopia is deliberate. The kitsch (rainbows, swans, peacock, balancing seals) is set up so that rusty, grimy engines can intrude and get blasted away, and that clash of material is the joke.
Each frame builds its type out of the world in a different way: topiary letters, letters on a peacock's tail, CHANGE spelled on balls balanced by seals. That is a typographic idea, not a caption.
The scenes are dense and full of characters. A flamingo swings a bat, a dog throws, a flock of engines flies off. Each frame shows a different gag, which points to real choreography and comic timing.
The dirty, photoreal engines against the glossy cartoon world show material contrast that someone directed on purpose.
gaps: Much of the frame is generic CG landscape (stock-feeling trees, clouds and water). D gets more out of every single frame with a tightly controlled graphic language.
The palette is the saturated rainbow cliché it is parodying. A more pointed grade could keep the satire and still show authorship.
The render finish varies from shot to shot (the dog and seals look cheaper than the engines). Lighting and shading need to hold together across the cast.

tells: The materials are worked hard: translucent sculpted hands, glowing coral, mesh and fibre, glassy tubes, wiry hair. Each surface is layered and textured, not a stock primitive.
The palettes are unusual and specific to each frame: rust ridge on pale pink, monochrome volcanic terrain with a magenta plume, sage on blue, bottle green with cyan.
Light motivates the frames: subsurface glow, a volcanic flare, specular sheen on the tubes.
gaps: There is no single idea. It plays like a reel or compilation of studio vignettes, each a different organic 3D sculpture, with no line through it. D has one concept carried through every shot.
The type is default sans name-tags ('Boldtron', 'Medusa Lab') dropped in the corner with no relationship to the image. It needs typography integrated into the world.
The 'organic-tech' maximal 3D look is close to current festival trends. It needs an image that only this piece could make.

tells: One idea runs through every frame: a silhouette chase that moves through worlds (park gate, alley seen from above, a vortex of spirals, a rooftop with a rocket). Each credit is staged as an event in the chase.

The type lives inside the scene. The director's name sits on the park gate's arch, ANDY SERKIS is lit on the pavement by a doorway's light cone, and the editor credit sits on the horizon. Every credit has its own placement.
Each scene has its own deliberate palette (dusty pink, aubergine and green, acid yellow-green, teal with oxblood figures), and flat graphic light still models depth with cast shadows and light pools.
The camera language varies widely (frontal, steep top-down, graphic spiral, wide horizon), which points to real choreography and pacing. Every frame works as a poster.
gaps: The 1960s Saul Bass/Pink Panther-style silhouette credits are a known reference, so it scores slightly lower on originality than on execution.
The typography is a single display caps style, consistent but conservative. More scale play between credits could push it further.
Some backgrounds (the trees in frame 1) are simpler than the figure animation. Texture could be more consistent across every layer.

tells: Deliberate, self-aware kitsch: a saccharine rainbow paradise invaded by rusty, photoreal engine blocks. The clash is the idea and reads as satire, not as a lack of taste

Lettering is built from the world itself (topiary letters, peacock-feather eyes spelling a word, seals balancing 'CHANGE' balls), so the type is integrated into the image rather than laid on top of it
A clear story across the frames: idyll, intrusion (a flamingo swinging a bat at an engine), a swarm of engines, a dog reacting. That is choreography and escalation, not one repeated layout
Mixed materials (photographic grime on the engines against glossy toy-like CG) are a deliberate contrast
Holding it back: dated mid-2000s CG finish, flat sky-dome lighting, busy compositions with no clear hierarchy
gaps: Commit to a graphic system: C reduces every frame to a few flat silhouettes and one dominant shape. A's frames scatter the eye across a dozen props
Light it with intent: the bright, even sky light flattens everything. Use motivated key light and shadow to stage the engines' arrival as a threat
Give the type a real typographic voice. The novelty letterforms (balls, hedges) are gags, not a designed face with scale contrast the way C sets its credits inside the action

defects: The end card's info block is set in a tiny monospace, about 10px cap height at 1080p. It reads as fine print and won't survive mobile or festival projection.

The 'ink on ink' Venn overlap is not a true overprint. Yellow and blue already make green, and then a separate muddy brown disc is dropped on top. That breaks the riso logic the film is selling, and the white label on it is low-contrast and generic.
The secondary column ('risograph / 3 inks / 120 tables') fades in at near-zero opacity, so in mid-transition frames it reads as a ghost or rendering error rather than a deliberate build.
The final ~2s is almost static (change/s 20.7 then 1.2), and the longest shot is 2.9s. The lockup holds without a reason beyond the music tail.
The halftone is a perfectly regular digital dot grid with uniform dot gain and no screen-angle variation between inks. It looks like a filter, not a print, and risks moiré on downscale.
The type misregistration (a pink offset behind the purple) is identical in every shot. It's a fixed drop-shadow, not live registration drift.
gaps: Motion lacks physical weight and the print metaphor. Sheets and shapes slide or drop in with generic easing. There's no drum feed, no ink laydown, no layer-by-layer registration build, so the riso process is pictured but never enacted in the movement. Transitions are hard wipes and pattern cuts, not handoffs where one ink layer becomes the next shot.

The sound is a static, looping synth bed: an evenly spaced transient grid every ~0.28s, the same few stacked harmonics bar after bar, flat dynamics, and one crash tail at ~7.8s. There's no paper or printer sound design (drum whir, sheet slaps, roller clicks), no drop-out before the reveal, and no clear hit landing on the date or title card beyond the beat grid.

The finish stays flat and digital. There's no paper tooth, uneven ink density, edge bleed or light falloff, and type properties carry no meaning: weight, offset and size never encode anything like ink count or layering. Top studio work would make the misregistration, overprint colour mixing and grain the actual storytelling device and keep the ending alive instead of holding a static card.
